title: The VA Sole-Sourced Its Core EHR Modernization Contract to Cerner. GAO Reported $9.4 Billion Obligated. After Patient Safety Events, It Halted Deployments in 2023.
subtitle: SOLE SOURCE. $9.4 BILLION. HALTED.
subject: Oracle Health / VA / Doug Collins
hook: In May 2018, the VA bypassed competition and awarded Cerner a sole-source contract for its entire electronic health record system. GAO reported $9.4 billion obligated by March 2023. After the VA's own Inspector General documented patient safety events at deployed sites, VA halted all future deployments in April 2023.
cold_open: A sole-source contract. No competitive bidding. The justification: only Cerner could deliver a system compatible with the Department of Defense's records. GAO reported $9.4 billion obligated by March 2023. By April 2023, after the VA's own Inspector General documented patient safety events at live sites, the VA halted all future deployments.

article_sections.heading: The rule
article_sections.body: The Federal Acquisition Regulation permits agencies to bypass competitive bidding under a set of defined exceptions. FAR 6.302-1 authorises a sole-source award when only one responsible source exists and no other supplies or services will satisfy the agency's requirements. Agencies that invoke FAR 6.302-1 are required to prepare a written Justification and Approval documenting why competition is not feasible. The rule is a legitimate statutory tool, designed for cases where competition is genuinely impossible. What it removes is the price discipline and independent evaluation that competitive bidding would otherwise provide. For a programme of this scale, the absence of that check is itself worth scrutiny.

article_sections.heading: The contract
article_sections.body: In May 2018, the Department of Veterans Affairs awarded a 10-year, sole-source contract to Cerner Corporation for an Electronic Health Record Modernisation programme, known as EHRM. The VA's Justification and Approval cited FAR 6.302-1, asserting Cerner as the only responsible source capable of meeting the requirement. A central rationale was interoperability: the Department of Defense had already selected Cerner for its own EHR programme, MHS GENESIS, and the VA argued that using the same system would enable seamless record-sharing between DoD and VA facilities. In June 2022, Oracle Corporation completed its acquisition of Cerner, and the VA contract transitioned to Oracle Health. GAO reported that VA had obligated approximately $9.4 billion on EHRM from FY2020 through March 2023.

article_sections.heading: The deployment record
article_sections.body: The VA originally planned to deploy the new EHR across more than 140 VA medical centres over the contract period. The first go-live occurred at Mann-Grandstaff VA Medical Center in Spokane, Washington, in October 2020. Subsequent deployments proceeded on a limited schedule, and clinical staff at deployed sites reported significant workflow disruptions. By April 2023, when the VA halted all future go-live events, GAO confirmed that only five VA sites were using the system. The VA announced it would focus on improving performance at those sites before resuming deployments. As of April 2026, the Federal EHR is live at ten VA medical centres. VA reporting indicates that deployments in Michigan are back on track, with additional go-lives scheduled through 2026. Against an original target of more than 140 sites, ten live deployments after eight years represents a programme still well behind its original schedule.

article_sections.heading: The patient safety record
article_sections.body: The VA Office of Inspector General conducted multiple reviews of EHRM implementation outcomes. OIG testimony in September 2022 indicated the OIG had reviewed whether the new EHR resulted in patient harm at deployed sites. The OIG documented patient safety events that reviewers determined were potentially related to EHR-associated issues. OIG testimony in February 2024 referenced an upcoming OIG report on an appointment-scheduling failure that contributed to the death of a patient. The OIG also found that clinical staff at deployed facilities experienced significant difficulties navigating the new system during patient care, and that certain medication and alert workflows created conditions for error. The OIG issued remediation recommendations, and VA leadership concurred. Whether those recommendations have been fully implemented is documented in subsequent OIG follow-up work.

article_sections.heading: Why it matters
article_sections.body: The central problem with the EHRM programme is not that Oracle Health is a bad company or that electronic health record modernisation is the wrong goal. The Veterans Health Information Systems and Technology Architecture, known as VistA, which the new system replaces, is genuinely outdated. The problem is that a procurement conducted without competition, at a scale of billions of dollars, has produced a system that was paused after five sites deployed, criticised by the agency's own Inspector General for patient safety failures, and is still well below its original deployment target eight years into the contract. Congressional oversight has been substantial: the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs has held multiple hearings. The GAO has issued reports. The OIG has made recommendations. No public competitive re-evaluation of the sole-source determination has been announced, based on available congressional and programme records.

article_sections.heading: What needs to change
article_sections.body: The VA does not need to abandon EHR modernisation. VistA's limitations are real, and the long-term case for a modern, interoperable record system serving veterans is sound. What the current programme requires is accountability proportionate to its scale and its record. First, the continuing sole-source justification should be reviewed: the original DoD-compatibility rationale was written in 2018, before years of documented performance failures. The landscape has changed. Second, the OIG's patient safety recommendations should be independently verified as implemented before each new deployment. Third, Congress has appropriated the funds. The VA owes its oversight committees a clear public account of what $9.4 billion has delivered, what the path to full deployment looks like, and what it will cost to reach the original scope. Eight years in, that account has not been given.
